Saptamātṛkās
(‘seven goddesses’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Durgāsaptaśatī, one of the basic texts on the मोथेर्-cult, when Kauśikī दुर्गा was fighting the demon Raktabīja—whose blood, if spilled, could produce demons similar to him—she manifested out of herself seven emanations. These are usually called the Saptamātṛkas or the ‘Seven little Mothers’. They are ब्राह्मी (or ब्रह्माणी) Māheśvarī, कौमारी, वैष्णवी, वाराही, Nārasiṁhī and Aindrī (or इन्द्राणी). As their very names indicate, they are the Śaktis of ब्रह्मा, ईश्वर, कुमार (Skanda), विष्णु, Varāha, नरसिṁह and इन्द्र. Hence they have the same forms, weapons and vehicles as their lords. Since the देवी, according to the same work, was formed out of the combined energies of all gods, this theory of the Saptamātṛkas becomes intelligible to us.
Sometimes, Nārasiṁhī is substituted by चामुण्डा (or Cāmuṇḍī). Along with the original deity—called दुर्गा Mahālakṣmī—they are counted as eight.
Sometimes, an esoteric interpretation is given by the followers of Tantraśāstra, with regard to these seven mātṛkās. ब्राह्मी, according to them represents the primordial नाद, the energy in which even the first throb has not yet appeared. This is the unmanifest sound (logos), the origin of all च्रेअतिओन्. It is the same as the substance or energy represented by the प्रणव (Om). When ब्राह्मी creates the universe, the power of वैष्णवी gives it a definite shape. The symmetry, beauty, organisation and order in the universe are the work of वैष्णवी. Māheśvarī stands for the power that gives individuality to the created beings. She resides in the hearts of all and makes them play, like the dolls mounted on a machine. कौमारी, the ever youthful deity, represents the ever present force of aspiration of the evolving सोउल्. She is Guruguhā (Guruguha being one of the names of कुमार or स्कन्द whose energy she is), the ‘guru’ (guide, teacher) in the ‘guhā’ (the cave of the heart, the intellect). वाराही is the all-consuming power of assimilation and enjoyment. Because of her, the living beings get their ड़ोओद् and all physical enjoyments. Aindrī or इन्द्राणी symbolises the terrible power that destroys all that opposes the cosmic law. चामुण्डा is the force of concentrated awareness, the power of spiritual awakening in the heart, that devours the ceaseless activity of the immature मिन्द् and uplifts it to the highest level. Raktabījāsura is actually the मिन्द्, each wave of which gives rise to other waves. Killing of this Raktabījā by चामुण्डा means the destruction of the mental modifications by the awakening of spiritual चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
These deities are generally represented as red in colour and with two hands, holding a skull and a lotus. However, since they are Śaktis of the above-mentioned gods, they are shown more often as female replicas of the male deities.
Sometimes each deity is assigned a tree as specially sacred to it. For instance: Udumbara (fig tree) for कौमारी, अश्वत्थ (peepal tree) for वैष्णवी and the Karañja (Indian beech) for वाराही.
They are usually grouped together with गणेश and वीरभद्र flanking on either side and shown on panels in the शिव temples. Occasionally they have a separate shrine built for them. The order or arrangement varies according to the effect desired. If the safety of the village is desired ब्राह्मी is installed in the centre. If increase in the population is the goal, चामुण्डा occupies the central place.

Saptapurī
(‘the seven [sacred] cities’)
------------------------------------------
The following seven cities were considered great places of पिल्ग्रिमगे: Avantī, अयोध्या, द्वारका, हरिद्वार, काञ्चीपुरम्, काशी and मथुरा.
See under each title for details.

śapatha
(‘special oath’)
------------------------------------------
In the ancient days, when a king could not decide whether a person brought before him as guilty was really guilty or not, due to lack of direct or circumstantial evidence, he could take to two methods; दिव्य (divine proof through ordeals) and शपथ (oath). (See DIVYA for its details.)
A शपथ is actually an oath taken by the accused to prove his innocence. Instances of śapathas are found in the Ṛgveda (7.104.15, 16), the epics (Mahā-bhārata, Anuśāsanaparva 95.13-35) and the smṛtis.
For example, वसिष्ठ when accused, declares in the Ṛgveda (7.104.15, 16), ‘If I am a यातुधान (sorcerer), may I die this very day!’ This is a शपथ.
The king in such cases of śapathas had to wait for a week or the stipulated period, whichever is less, to know the result.

saptasādhana
(‘sevenfold spiritual path’)
------------------------------------------
The works on हठयोग like the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā (1.9) describe seven exercises for purifying the body and the मिन्द्, and making it fit for yogic sādhana.
They are: śodhana (purification); dṛḍhatā (strengthening); sthairya (steadiness); dhairya (steadiness produced by the restraint of the senses); लाघव (lightness); प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception); and, nirlipti (isolation).

sapiṇḍīkaraṇa
(‘grouping together’)
------------------------------------------
Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa (or sapiṇḍana) is the reception of the dead person’s सोउल् into the community of the पितृस् or forefathers.
The process is actually a śrāddha (obsequial rite) and can be done on any of the following days after death: 12th day; 4th month; 6th month; 11th month; or after a year.
The first seems to be more common.
The important steps are: invitation to the ब्राह्मणस् the previous day; agnau-karaṇa (See AGNAUKARAṆA for details.); recital of Vedic texts when the ब्राह्मणस् are eating; keeping four vessels of water with कुश grass (one for the dead ancestor [called प्रेत now] and the other three for the पितृस्) and mixing the water of the first with the water of the other three with appropriate mantras. This completes the process of merging the प्रेत with the पितृस् of पितृलोक.

saptapadī
(‘[the rite of taking] seven steps [together]’)
------------------------------------------
See VIVĀHA.

saptajñānabhūmikā
(‘seven preparatory stages for attaining knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
The Varāha Upaniṣad (

-17) describes seven bhūmikās or preparatory stages for obtaining knowledge. They are as follows:
1. Śubhecchā (= sincere desire)
This is the sincere desire that arises in the मिन्द् of a seeker, as a result of the study of the śāstras (scriptures) and company of the holy, to know his real nature.
2. Vicāraṇā (= enquiry)
The enquiry (born out of śubhecchā) that leads the seeker to be inclined towards good conduct is vicāraṇā.
3. Tanumānasī (= attenuation of the मिन्द्)
The first two stages when practised well, make the मिन्द् (= mānasa), thin or attenuated (= tanu). Such a मिन्द् will not get attached to sense-objects.
4. Sattvāpatti (= attaining सत्त्व)
This is the state of being established—though indirectly—in the आत्मन् (the individual Self), who is सत्त्व (the pure, the real). This is attained as a result of practising the earlier three stages.
5. Asaṁsakti (= non-attachment)
In this state the sādhaka is completely unattached to experiences that come in life whether good or bad,
6. Padarthabhāvanā (= becoming aware of objects [through others])
When the seeker reaches this state, he is not aware of padārthas or objects (whether they are inside or outside himself) and has to be made aware of them by others. The reason is that his मिन्द् is always dwelling on his

. Turyagā (= entering into the ‘fourth’, i.e., the आत्मन्)
In this final state, the seeker’s चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् transcends all duality and is well-established in the आत्मन् or the Self.
It should be noted that each stage leads to the next, if practised properly.

Saptarṣis
(‘the seven sages’)
------------------------------------------
The epics and the पुराणस् often mention the सप्तर्षिस्, the seven sages, who are highly praised.
Generally two sets of सप्तर्षिस् are named, as belonging to two different manvantaras (periods of मनु).
The sages of वैवस्वत-मन्वन्तर are: अत्रि, भरद्वाज, गौतम, जमदग्नि, कश्यप, वसिष्ठ and विश्वामित्र.
The sages of Svāyambhuvamanvantara are: Aṅgirasa, अत्रि, Kratu, मरीचि, Pulaha, पुलस्त्य and वसिष्ठ.
Even now a group of seven bright स्तर्स् of the constellation of Great Bear is identified with them.

saptadvīpas
(‘the seven islands’)
------------------------------------------
The geography of this earth as described in the पुराणस् is—though enigmatic—interesting.
Originally the whole earth was one landmass. The sun was traversing always on one side of it leaving the other side eternally dark. So, the great king Priya-vrata (considered an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु, who established organised human dwellings for the first time) drove his chariot round on earth, in seven concentric circles, thus creating seven dvīpas or islands and seven samudras or oceans. The following are the details:
1. Jambūdvīpa
This is the first of the seven islands and is spread round the mountain मेरु which is the axis. It is surrounded by the lavaṇasamudra, the ocean of salt-water.
Āgnīdhra, the eldest son of Priyavrata was its first ruler.
He later on divided it into nine khaṇḍas or parts or continents and gave it to his nine sons. These came to be known as varṣas in their names such as Ajanābhavarṣa, Kimpuruṣavarṣa, Harivarṣa and so on.
2. Plakṣadvīpa
Second of the seven islands, it is surrounded by the ikṣusamudra, the ocean of sugarcane juice.
Idhmajihva, the second son of Priya-vrata, was its first king.
3. Śālmalīdvīpa
This is the third island, surrounded by surāsamudra, the ocean of wine.
The first ruler was Yajñabāhu.
4. Kuśadvīpa
This is the fourth of the seven islands and is surrounded by ghṛtasamudra, the ocean of ghee. Hiraṇyaretas was its first monarch.
5. Krauñcadvīpa
This island, surrounded by the sea of curds, was ruled by Ghṛtapṛṣṭha the fifth son of

. Śākadvīpa
Encircled by the sea of milk, Śāka-द्वीप, the sixth island, was administered by मेधातिथि.
7. Puṣkaradvīpa
Surrounded by the ocean of pure water, this island had Vītihotra as its first king.
These seven islands have been identified by Indologists as follows: जम्बूद्वीप = Asia; Plakṣadvīpa = South America; Śālmalīdvīpa = Australia; कुश-द्वीप = Oceania; Krauñcadvīpa = Africa; Śākadvīpa (not identified); Puṣkaradvīpa = North America.

saptasamudra
(‘seven seas or oceans’)
------------------------------------------
See SĀGARA.

saptārcis
(‘seven flames’)
------------------------------------------
In the śrāddha ceremonies, not only the Vedic but also the purāṇic mantras are recited at the appropriate places. The सप्तार्चिस् मन्त्र in which the देवतास् (gods), पितृस् (manes), great yogins, the goddesses स्वधा and स्वाहा are adored, is to be recited thrice at the beginning and the end of śrāddha as also at the time of offering piṇḍas. As a result, the पितृस् come quickly and the goblins are supposed to run away.
This मन्त्र occurs in the Vāyupurāṇa (74.15, 16), the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (3.11.17, 18), the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (1.140.68) and a few other पुराणस्.

sapiṇḍa
(‘of the same body’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu धर्मशास्त्रस् have stipulated many conditions for the मर्रिअगे of a boy with a girl, both of marriageable age. One important rule in this series is that they should not be सपिण्ड.
Sapiṇḍa literally means having the same body-particles. For instance, a ड़थेर् and a son or a daughter, are सपिण्ड since the particles of the body of the ड़थेर् exist in the bodies of both.
This सपिण्ड relationship extends up to seven generations in the lineage of the ड़थेर् and up to five generations in the lineage of the मोथेर्. मर्रिअगे within this सपिण्ड relationship is prohibited.
See also GOTRA and SAGOTRA.

saptabhūmikās
(‘seven stages [of ascent’}
------------------------------------------
The तन्त्रस् describe seven bhūmikās or ācāras—gradually increasing stages or steps—by which a spiritual aspirant rises to the highest level of spiritual illumination. They are: veda, vaiṣṇava, śaiva, dakṣiṇa, vāma, सिद्धान्त and कौल. They are also termed as vedācāra, vaiṣṇavācāra and so on.
Veda is the daily practice of the religious rites prescribed by the scriptures in accordance with the वेदस्.
Vaiṣṇava is the cultivation of devotion to God.
Śaiva is adding ज्ञान or knowledge also to the sādhana or spiritual practice.
Dakṣiṇa is the fourth stage wherein the gains of the first three stages are consolidated by meditation on the three aspects of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् viz., सरस्वती, लक्ष्मी and पार्वती.
Vāma, the fifth stage is that of निवृत्ति or renunciation.
Siddhānta is the sixth stage in which the aspirant comes to definite conclusions about the relative merits of the two paths of pravṛtti (activism, enjoyment) and निवृत्ति (withdrawal, renunciation), and, decides to pursue the latter path.
Kaula, the last stage, is the state of realisation of कुल or ब्रह्मन्.
